tagline: Music-making studio in the browser with live collaboration.
verdictSummary: Mature open-source digital audio workstations exist and outclass Soundtrap on recording, editing and mixing. Two things do not carry over. The first is real-time collaboration — two people editing the same session while talking to each other — which is the classic gap in this catalogue and is genuinely hard. The second is the loop and instrument library, which is licensed content, not software.
coreLoopDIY: Record and arrange multitrack audio and MIDI locally in a full desktop workstation, and share sessions as files rather than as a live document.
whatYouLose: two people editing the same session at the same time
thousands of licensed loops and one-shots cleared for release
running in a browser on a school Chromebook with nothing installed
the project living in the cloud, reachable from any machine
whyPeopleStillPay: For a classroom or a band spread across three cities, the collaboration and the zero-install browser session are the product, and a local workstation replaces neither.
prompt:
Set up a local music production workflow around an open-source digital audio workstation, and solve the collaboration half with version control rather than pretending to solve it live.

Install Ardour for audio-led work or LMMS for pattern-led production. Do not build a workstation.

The project that is worth writing is the session-sharing layer. Put each project in a git repository with git-lfs for audio, and write a small tool that: prepares a session for sharing by consolidating every referenced sample into the project folder (the classic failure is a session that opens with missing files on someone else's machine); records the plugin list with versions into a manifest; and refuses to commit if any plugin is not in a shared, agreed list.

Add a bounce-on-commit hook that renders a stereo mixdown to an `exports/` folder named after the commit. That gives every collaborator a listenable version of every revision without opening the project, which is most of what real-time collaboration is actually used for.

For loops, build a tagged local sample library over material you have licensed or recorded: a folder scanner that reads BPM and key from filenames or detects them, writes them into a SQLite index, and offers search by tempo range and key. Store the licence for each pack in the index, so "can I release this?" has an answer.

Do not implement live collaborative editing. Conflict-free concurrent editing of a timeline with audio is a research-grade problem and a half-working version loses takes.

faq.q: Can I get my Soundtrap projects out?
faq.a: Only as audio. Soundtrap exports mixdowns and, on paid tiers, individual track stems — but not a project file any other workstation can open. Export stems for anything you care about before cancelling, then rebuild the arrangement locally.

faq.q: Can I still work from a Chromebook?
faq.a: Not with this setup. Ardour and LMMS are desktop applications; if a locked-down machine is the constraint, Soundtrap solves a problem the local workflow does not.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing for the software. Audio in git-lfs on a hosted remote costs storage — a few dollars a month for a handful of projects, or nothing on a drive you already back up.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Two people in the same session at once. Commits and bounces are a good asynchronous substitute, and they are not the same as hearing someone move your fader while you talk about it.
